title: X.509 Internet Public Key Infrastructure Online Certificate Status Protocol - OCSP
summary: This document specifies the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP), a way to find out the current status of a digital certificate without Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs). It obsoletes RFCs 2560 and 6277 and updates RFC 5912.

plainLanguage.summary: The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) lets a client ask whether a digital certificate is good, revoked, or unknown to a responder. The signed answer includes times that help the client judge whether the information is current.

subtitle: A signed request-and-response protocol for checking the status of a digital certificate.

tldr.problem: A periodically published certificate revocation list may not provide status information quickly enough for some decisions. OCSP lets an application ask about identified certificates directly.
tldr.mechanism: An OCSP client identifies a certificate in a request. A responder returns a signed status and validity times, or an unsigned error if it cannot provide a definitive answer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6960 obsoletes RFC 2560 and RFC 6277, updates RFC 5912, and has been updated by RFC 8954 and RFC 9654.

today: RFC 6960 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2560 and RFC 6277, and updates RFC 5912. It has been updated by RFC 8954 and RFC 9654.

sections.title: Checking a Certificate's Current Status
sections.content:
OCSP determines the status of a digital certificate without requiring a Certificate Revocation List (CRL). It may provide more timely information than checking a periodic CRL, or supplement CRL checking. The RFC gives high-value funds transfers and large stock trades as examples where timely information may matter.

An OCSP client sends a status request to a responder and suspends acceptance of the certificate until it receives a response. RFC 6960 clarifies parts of the earlier specification, including when a responder is authorized and how the revoked status can apply to certificates that were never issued.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask a responder for the status of a certificate instead of relying only on a periodic revocation list. The client waits for the responder's answer before accepting the certificate.

sections.title: Requests, Responses, and Status Values
sections.content:
A request contains the protocol version, a service request, a certificate identifier, and optional extensions. The identifier includes a hash of the issuer's name, a hash of its public key, and the certificate serial number. The two issuer hashes help distinguish issuers that might use the same name.

A definitive response MUST be digitally signed and reports one of three statuses. good means, at a minimum, that no certificate with the requested serial number currently within its validity interval is revoked; it does not prove the certificate was ever issued. revoked means the certificate has been revoked or placed on hold, and unknown means the responder cannot determine its status.

The response includes status times. thisUpdate is when the status was last known to be correct, nextUpdate indicates when newer information will be available, and producedAt is when the responder signed the response. Clients should consider responses outside their stated validity interval unreliable.
sections.plainLanguage: The client identifies a certificate by its issuer and serial number. The responder signs a status of good, revoked, or unknown and includes times that show how fresh the answer is.

sections.title: The OCSP Request and Response
sections.content:
OCSP messages use ASN.1 syntax, and signed data uses Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). An OCSPRequest contains a request body and may include a signature. Each certificate request includes a CertID with a hash algorithm, issuer-name hash, issuer-key hash, and serial number.

An OCSPResponse begins with a response status. On success, it includes response bytes; the basic response type MUST be supported by all responders and clients. The basic response identifies the responder, gives a production time, includes a response for each requested certificate, and carries a signature.

The response signer must be authorized. It can be the issuing CA, a locally trusted responder, or a responder given signing authority by the CA through a specially marked certificate issued directly by that CA.
sections.plainLanguage: The request identifies the certificate being checked, and the response contains the result. A client must check both the response signature and whether its signer was authorized.

sections.title: When a Client Can Trust a Response
sections.content:
Before accepting a signed response, a client must check that it refers to the certificate in the request, that the signature is valid, and that the signer is the intended and authorized responder. The client also checks that thisUpdate is recent enough and, when present, nextUpdate is later than the current time.

A CA can delegate OCSP signing authority by issuing a responder certificate with the id-kp-OCSPSigning extended key usage. That certificate must be issued directly by the CA named in the request. A CA can also specify how a responder's own certificate is checked for revocation, or leave that choice to the client's local security policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A client checks who signed the status and whether that signer is allowed to answer. It also checks that the answer's time information is acceptable.

sections.title: Errors Are Not Signed
sections.content:
If a responder cannot provide a definitive response, it can return an error. The defined errors are malformedRequest, internalError, tryLater, sigRequired, and unauthorized. They indicate problems such as invalid syntax, temporary inability to answer, a required request signature, or lack of authority.

Error messages are not signed. The RFC notes that this permits an attacker to send false error responses.
sections.plainLanguage: An error tells the client why the responder did not give a certificate status. Because errors are unsigned, they do not have the signature protection required for definitive answers.

sections.title: Optional Extensions
sections.content:
OCSP extensions are optional for clients and responders. The RFC defines extensions for a nonce that binds a request to its response, CRL references, acceptable response types, archive cutoff times, service location, preferred signature algorithms, and the extended revoked definition.

A nonce can help prevent replay by connecting a response to a request. A client can list its preferred signature algorithms in order, and a responder selects a supported algorithm under the RFC's rules. The extended revoked definition identifies responses that use revoked for certificates that were never issued.
sections.plainLanguage: Optional extensions add details such as a request-matching nonce or preferred signature algorithms. Both sides can use extensions that they support.

sections.title: Replay, Availability, and HTTP Transport
sections.content:
A flood of status queries can cause denial of service, and generating signatures adds work for a responder. Pre-produced responses can be replayed after a certificate is revoked but before the response expires. The RFC advises deployers to weigh the efficiency of pre-production against that risk.

Over HTTP, clients may use GET for requests shorter than 255 bytes after encoding; otherwise, or when caching is not important, the RFC recommends POST. HTTP caching can produce unexpected results if intermediate caches are misconfigured. When privacy is required, HTTP transactions may be protected using TLS/SSL or another lower-layer protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Old signed answers can be replayed while they remain valid, and a responder can be burdened by too many requests. HTTP caching and transport privacy also need attention when OCSP uses HTTP.
